items.item: Shuffle-read fetch wait time -- the time a task spends blocked waiting for shuffle data from remote executors -- is a sixth, distinct signature from the five this topic's own examples.py measures: a high value there points at network or remote-executor slowness, not at skew, spill, GC, small files, or an idle driver.

at.out: shuffle-read fetch wait time named only as a sixth distinct signature; this topic's own examples.py runs entirely in local mode, where remote-executor fetch wait is not representative of a real multi-node cluster

items.item: The Executors tab's own per-executor summary (task count, total duration, total GC time, shuffle read/write) is the fastest first check for a driver bottleneck specifically, since idle executors across the whole tab during a known-slow stretch are visible without opening any individual stage at all.

at.out: the Executors tab's own summary view named as the fastest entry point for the driver-bottleneck diagnosis; this topic's own examples.py confirms the same idle stretch via the REST API's per-stage task-time sum rather than the rendered tab itself

items.item: A stage's DAG visualization on the Jobs and Stages tabs shows which stages depend on which, so a driver bottleneck (time between two jobs) and a stage resubmission (extra attempts within one job) are visually distinguishable even before reading any task-level metric.

at.out: the DAG visualization's own role in telling a driver gap apart from a stage resubmission named only; this topic's own examples.py distinguishes them through REST API timestamps and stage-attempt counts, not the rendered DAG graph

items.item: Peak execution memory (the maximum memory used by internal shuffle/aggregation/join data structures during a task) is the metric that would show *why* a task spilled, complementing the spill-bytes columns this topic's own examples.py measures directly: a peak near the task's own memory budget explains the spill that the spill columns only report happened.

at.out: peak execution memory named as the explanatory metric behind an observed spill; this topic's own examples.py measures the spill event itself (bytes spilled to memory and disk), not the peak-memory metric that would explain why it happened

items.item: Compaction of rolling event log files (spark.eventLog.rolling.enabled) keeps a single long-running application's event log from becoming one huge file that's expensive for the History Server to replay -- a practical concern for diagnosing a job that ran for hours, distinct from any of the five failure modes this topic's own examples.py reproduces in a short-lived local session.

at.out: event-log rolling and compaction named only as a practical History Server concern for long-running applications; this topic's own examples.py runs short-lived local sessions where rolling never triggers

items.item: The number-of-output-rows SQL metric, shown per operator on the plan graph, is often the fastest way to confirm a small-files or over-partitioning diagnosis without touching the Stages tab at all: a Scan operator producing far more partitions than its own row count would justify is directly visible there.

at.out: the number-of-output-rows SQL metric named as a faster alternative confirmation path for the small-files diagnosis; this topic's own examples.py confirms small files through the Stages tab's own per-task scheduler-delay and CPU-time columns instead

items.item: A thread dump, available per executor from the Executors tab, shows exactly what every thread on that executor is doing at the moment it's captured -- the one tool in the Spark UI that can distinguish a task genuinely computing (a hot loop) from one blocked (on a lock, on I/O, on a remote fetch) when the task-metric columns alone look identical.

at.out: the per-executor thread dump named as the tool that resolves an ambiguous task-metric reading by showing what the thread is actually doing; this topic's own examples.py reads only aggregate REST API metrics, never a live thread dump

items.item: Associated accumulators, shown on a task's own details page when named accumulators exist, let a job author surface custom per-task counters (rows rejected by a filter, bytes read from a specific source) directly in the UI -- a sixth diagnostic surface beyond the five built-in failure modes this topic's own examples.py reproduces, available only when the job itself chose to instrument it.

at.out: named accumulators on the task details page named only as an author-instrumented diagnostic surface; this topic's own examples.py uses no named accumulators

items.item: WholeStageCodegen's own annotation in the SQL plan (a numbered id prefixing each fused physical operator) lets a reader cross-reference a specific stage's task metrics back to the exact block of fused operators that produced them, connecting the Stages tab's own per-task numbers to the SQL tab's own plan graph rather than treating the two tabs as unrelated views.

at.out: the WholeStageCodegen numbering as the cross-reference between the Stages tab and the SQL tab named only; this topic's own examples.py reads the Stages/Executors REST API directly and does not cross-reference a rendered SQL plan

items.item: spark.history.fs.cleaner.* configs let the History Server automatically delete old event logs past a retention window -- a practical operational concern for keeping years of diagnosable history bounded, distinct from any of this topic's own measured, single-session failure modes.

at.out: History Server log retention/cleaner configs named only as a separate operational concern from this topic's own single-session measurements
